strengths: Simple, elegant, and computationally lightweight idea: LayerSync regularizes diffusion/flow models using intra-model self-alignment with a stop-gradient, requiring no external pre-trained models (e.g., DINOv2, VLMs) or auxiliary EMA encoders, thereby avoiding extra inference overhead and memory footprint.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple modalities: In addition to class-conditional ImageNet generation (B, L, XL scales), the authors validate the method on audio synthesis (MTG-Jamendo), human motion generation (HumanML3D), and video generation/fine-tuning (CLEVRER, SSv2 with CogVideoX and Wan2.1).

Strong empirical performance and acceleration: On ImageNet 256x256, LayerSync consistently outperforms the self-contained baseline (Dispersive Loss) across scales and training lengths, achieving up to 8.75x speedup over the vanilla baseline and reaching competitive FID (1.89 at 800 epochs with CFG) close to methods leveraging massive external supervision.

Insightful representation and ablation analyses: Downstream linear probing (classification on Tiny ImageNet, segmentation on PASCAL VOC), CKA alignment to DINOv2, and random layer pairing ablations provide useful evidence that self-alignment systematically alters and improves internal feature hierarchies.
weaknesses: Limited theoretical and mechanistic grounding: The core premise—that an earlier layer learns from a later layer that itself depends on the earlier layer via stop-gradient—is intuitively intriguing but lacks formal or mechanistic analysis. Further investigation into optimization dynamics, feature rank, or gradient behavior would help clarify why this does not lead to representational collapse or trivial identity solutions.

Inconsistency in loss formulation across modalities: While cosine similarity is used for images, audio, and motion, the video experiments switch to the TRD loss from Zhang et al. (2025). This weakens the claim of a completely universal, parameter-free plug-and-play loss across all domains.

Exploration restricted to single-pair alignment: The method only investigates aligning a single pair of layers (k, k'). It remains unclear whether aligning multiple intermediate layers simultaneously (e.g., progressive or hierarchical alignment) could further improve performance or if it over-constrains network representations.

Minor presentation flaws and typographical errors: The manuscript contains noticeable typos (e.g., 'comapre' on page 5, 'R-Percision' on pages 7 and 19, 'representtaion' on page 14) that detract from the final polish.

strengths: Simple, elegant, and self-contained: LayerSync does not require external foundation models (like DINOv2 or VLMs) or EMA teacher networks, eliminating extra parameter memory and forward/backward inference overhead.

Comprehensive empirical validation across modalities: The paper validates the approach not only on standard ImageNet class-conditional generation across various model sizes (SiT-B, L, XL), but also extends it to audio generation (MTG-Jamendo), text-conditioned human motion generation (HumanML3D), and video generation/fine-tuning (CLEVRER, CogVideoX, Wan2.1).

Strong efficiency and quality gains: LayerSync achieves an impressive ~8.75x training acceleration on ImageNet 256x256 to reach comparable baseline FID, clearly outperforming the recent self-contained Dispersive Loss baseline.

Insightful representation and ablation analyses: The paper provides probing results (Tiny ImageNet classification, PASCAL VOC segmentation, CKA similarity to DINOv2), layer pairing sensitivity checks, hyperparameter sweeps, and block-dropping experiments, demonstrating good robustness and empirical grounding.
weaknesses: Incomplete theoretical understanding of collapse avoidance: The paper relies on stopgrad to prevent collapse, but deeper theoretical analysis is lacking on why forcing shallow layers to align with deep layers does not collapse the representational capacity across the depth or hurt hierarchical abstraction.

Inconsistency in loss definition for video experiments: For video generation in Appendix A, the authors switch from patch-level cosine similarity to the spatio-temporal TRD loss from VideoREPA. While justified empirically, this departs from the claim of a completely domain-agnostic, single alignment formulation without clear ablation against simple cosine similarity on spatio-temporal tokens.

Restriction to single-pair alignment: The paper only evaluates aligning a single chosen pair of layers $(k, k')$. Exploring multi-layer or dense self-alignment would clarify whether additional internal guidance provides diminishing or compounding returns.

Remaining gap to external guidance methods: While LayerSync outperforms self-contained baselines, there is still a noticeable performance and convergence gap compared to models guided by heavy external models (e.g., REED reaching FID 1.80 in 200 epochs versus LayerSync reaching 1.89 at 800 epochs).

strengths: Simple, elegant, and practical method: LayerSync proposes an intra-model intermediate layer self-alignment regularizer that is parameter-free, requires no external foundation models (e.g., DINOv2, VLMs) or EMA teacher forward passes, and introduces virtually zero computational overhead.

Broad cross-modal evaluation: Beyond standard class-conditional ImageNet generation (across multiple model capacities: SiT-B, SiT-L, SiT-XL), the authors validate LayerSync across audio (MTG-Jamendo), text-to-motion (HumanML3D), and video generation/fine-tuning (CogVideoX, Wan2.1, SiT-XL on CLEVRER).

Strong empirical gains: Achieves notable speedups and quality improvements, outperforming the primary zero-overhead baseline (Dispersive loss) significantly and narrowing the performance gap with methods that rely on heavy external pre-trained representations (reaching an FID of 1.89 on ImageNet 256x256).

Insightful representation and ablation analysis: The paper provides probing experiments (linear classification on Tiny ImageNet, segmentation on PASCAL VOC, CKA similarity to DINOv2), block-dropping experiments, PCA visualizations, and evaluates sensitivity to layer selection (10 random pairings) and regularizer weighting.
weaknesses: Contextualization within the broader self-distillation literature: Aligning shallow layer features with deeper layer representations (self-distillation / deep supervision, e.g., 'Be Your Own Teacher', 'Born Again Networks') is a classical concept in deep learning. While its application to diffusion/flow-based transformers is novel and timely, the conceptual connection to prior intra-network self-distillation works should be more thoroughly discussed.

Loss formulation discrepancy across modalities: While cosine similarity is used for images, audio, and motion, the video experiments in Appendix A adopt the TRD relational loss. This indicates that vanilla patch-wise cosine similarity may not be entirely sufficient across all domains, qualifying the claim of a completely universal, off-the-shelf formulation.

Exploration of multi-layer alignment: The method restricts itself to syncing a single pair of layers $(k, k')$. It remains unclear whether aligning multiple intermediate layers simultaneously (e.g., progressive ladder alignment) yields further benefits or causes over-regularization / feature collapse.

Minor presentation and typographical issues: There are several minor typos throughout the draft (e.g., 'comapre' on page 5, 'Percision' in Table 4 and Section 4.3/H.1, and 'representtaion' on page 14).

strengths: Simple, elegant, and self-contained approach: LayerSync requires no external pretrained models, no additional learnable parameters, and no extra forward passes (unlike EMA-teacher approaches), introducing virtually zero computational overhead.

Strong empirical gains and training acceleration: On ImageNet 256x256, LayerSync achieves an 8.75x speedup to match baseline FID and significantly outperforms existing self-contained regularizers like Dispersive Loss and SRA, while narrowing the gap with methods relying on external guidance (e.g., REPA, REED).

Cross-modal versatility: Unlike foundation-model-guided approaches that are largely restricted to natural images, LayerSync is domain-agnostic and demonstrated to consistently boost generation quality across audio (MTG-Jamendo), text-to-motion (HumanML3D), and video (CLEVRER and Wan2.1 fine-tuning).

Thorough empirical analysis and ablations: The paper provides insightful probing experiments (linear classification, semantic segmentation, CKA alignment with DINOv2), confirms the 'virtuous cycle' hypothesis, rules out trivial explanations such as effective learning rate increases via gradient norm analysis, and conducts exhaustive layer-pairing ablations.
weaknesses: Heuristic layer selection: While the paper presents clear principles and demonstrates reasonable robustness across random layer pairs, selecting the optimal pair of layers (k, k') still relies on empirical heuristics tailored to the specific architecture depth.

Limited theoretical formulation: The conceptual explanation relies primarily on intuitive hypotheses ('virtuous cycle', structural equilibrium) and empirical visualizations; a more rigorous theoretical or optimization-level understanding of why intra-model alignment avoids representation collapse without contrastive negative pairs remains an open question.

Scope of generation tasks: While the multi-modal evaluations are commendable, the image generation experiments are primarily confined to class-conditional ImageNet 256x256; evaluating on large-scale open-domain text-to-image benchmarks would further substantiate scalability.

strengths: The core idea of LayerSync is simple, elegant, and practically appealing: it achieves representation guidance entirely internally by aligning shallow layer representations with deeper, semantically richer layers via a stop-gradient cosine similarity loss, requiring no external teacher models, no EMA copies, and virtually zero computational overhead.

The empirical results on ImageNet class-conditional generation are very strong: LayerSync significantly accelerates convergence (up to 8.75× speedup to match baseline FID), consistently outperforms existing self-contained regularizers like Dispersive Loss and SRA, and narrows the performance gap to external guidance methods (REPA/REED).

The method demonstrates true domain and modality generality, exhibiting clear improvements across audio generation (MTG-Jamendo), human motion generation (HumanML3D), and video generation/fine-tuning (CLEVRER / Wan2.1), domains where pre-trained foundation models are often unavailable or cumbersome to integrate.

The paper includes thorough diagnostic analyses and ablations, including linear probing on downstream tasks (classification and semantic segmentation), CKA alignment with DINOv2, gradient norm comparisons against learning-rate scaling baselines, and extensive layer-pair ablations across model scales.
weaknesses: While the layer selection heuristic (avoiding the first few layers and the final 20% decoding blocks, while maintaining a minimum layer distance) is empirically supported, selecting the optimal layer pair remains an empirical discrete hyperparameter that must be adapted across different architectures and depths.

The theoretical understanding of the mechanism remains mostly qualitative and intuitive; while the 'virtuous cycle' hypothesis is supported empirically through probing experiments, a formal explanation of why stop-gradient alignment across depth avoids degenerative representations in diffusion transformers is left largely unexplored.

While the ImageNet evaluation is extensive, the non-image experiments (audio, motion, and video) are evaluated on relatively smaller scales or fewer iterations/baselines, serving primarily as proofs of concept.

strengths: Simple, elegant, and self-contained design: LayerSync eliminates the need for massive external pretrained vision models (e.g., DINOv2, VLMs) or EMA teacher forward passes by using internal intermediate representation alignment with a stop-gradient operator, introducing virtually no computational or parameter overhead.

Strong empirical performance and acceleration: On ImageNet 256x256, the method accelerates diffusion transformer (SiT-XL) training by ~8.75x to match baseline quality and achieves a competitive FID of 1.49 (with CFG scheduling), outperforming prior self-contained regularizers like Dispersive loss.

Compelling cross-modal generality: Unlike vision-specific guidance techniques, the self-contained formulation transfers across diverse data domains, demonstrating consistent improvements on audio generation (MTG-Jamendo), human motion synthesis (HumanML3D), and video generation (CLEVRER / Wan2.1).

Thorough representation probing and diagnostic analyses: The paper provides in-depth empirical validation including downstream linear probing (Tiny ImageNet classification, PASCAL VOC segmentation), CKA alignment with DINOv2, layer-dropping robustness, gradient norm comparisons against higher learning rates, and combinations with REPA.
weaknesses: Heuristic layer selection: While the ablation studies show that performance improvements are relatively robust across various layer pairings, optimal gains still rely on empirical heuristics (e.g., skipping the first few layers, avoiding the last 20% decoding layers, and maintaining a minimum layer distance). An automated, adaptive, or depth-continuous formulation is not investigated.

Lack of formal theoretical grounding: The explanation for why LayerSync accelerates convergence relies primarily on the intuitive hypothesis of an internal 'virtuous cycle' and empirical observations. A deeper theoretical or optimization perspective explaining why this alignment avoids harmful representational bottlenecks or premature collapse would strengthen the paper.

Limited exploration of multi-pair or scheduled alignment: The current method predominantly restricts alignment to a single designated pair of layers throughout the entire training process; investigating multi-layer alignment schemes or dynamic loss schedules across training steps remains underexplored.
